Peripheral Vascular Disease

1. Definition and Overview

Peripheral Vascular Disease (PVD) is a circulatory disorder in which the blood vessels outside the heart and brain become narrowed, blocked, or dilated. The epidemiology of PVD shows that it affects approximately 10 million people in the United States, with an incidence of 500,000 new cases per year. The prevalence increases with age, affecting 5% of people at age 50 and 20% at age 70. The causes of PVD include:
  • Atherosclerosis: the buildup of plaque in the arteries
  • Thrombosis: the formation of blood clots in the blood vessels
  • Emboli: the blockage of blood vessels by foreign particles or blood clots
  • Inflammation: the swelling of blood vessels due to infection or injury
  • Genetic disorders: inherited conditions that affect blood vessel development

2. Classification / Types

The classification of PVD is based on the location and severity of the disease. The main types of PVD are:
Type Features Examples
Arterial PVD Narrowing or blockage of arteries Peripheral artery disease (PAD), carotid artery disease
Venous PVD Dilation or blockage of veins Varicose veins, deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
Lymphatic PVD Blockage or damage to lymphatic vessels Lymphedema

3. Pathophysiology / Mechanism

The pathophysiology of PVD involves the following steps:
  1. The buildup of plaque in the arteries, which can be caused by high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and smoking
  2. The narrowing of the arteries, which can lead to ischemia (reduced blood flow) and hypoxia (reduced oxygen delivery)
  3. The formation of blood clots, which can block the blood vessels and cause thrombosis
  4. The activation of inflammatory cells, which can cause inflammation and further damage to the blood vessels
  5. The measurement of ankle-brachial index (ABI): 0.9-1.4 to diagnose PVD

4. Clinical Features / Signs and Symptoms

The clinical features of PVD include: Cardinal symptoms:
  • Intermittent claudication: pain in the legs or arms during exercise
  • Rest pain: pain in the legs or arms at rest
  • Ulcers: open sores on the skin that do not heal
Early features:
  • Fatigue
  • Weakness
  • Numbness
Late features:
  • Gangrene: death of tissue due to lack of blood supply
  • Amputation: surgical removal of a limb

5. Diagnosis

The diagnosis of PVD involves: ABI: 0.9-1.4 Doppler ultrasound: normal range Angiography: normal range Imaging tests:
  • Computed tomography (CT) scan
  • Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan
Special tests:
  • Exercise stress test
  • Treadmill test

6. Management / Treatment

The management of PVD involves: Medical management: Aspirin: 81-325 mg PO daily Clopidogrel: 75 mg PO daily Statins: simvastatin 20-40 mg PO daily Surgical management:
  1. Angioplasty: a minimally invasive procedure to widen the arteries
  2. Stenting: a procedure to place a stent in the artery to keep it open
  3. Bypass surgery: a surgical procedure to bypass the blocked artery

7. Nursing Care

The nursing care of PVD involves: Nursing assessment checklist:
  • Vital signs
  • Medical history
  • Physical examination
NANDA nursing diagnoses:
  • Activity intolerance
  • Pain
  • Anxiety
Nursing interventions:
  • Exercise program
  • Smoking cessation
  • Dietary counseling
Patient education points:
  • Importance of exercise
  • Importance of quitting smoking
  • Importance of healthy diet

8. Complications

The complications of PVD include:
  • Gangrene
  • Amputation
  • Myocardial infarction
Emergency complications:
  • Aortic aneurysm
  • Aortic dissection
Immediate management:
  1. Call 911
  2. Administer oxygen
  3. Administer pain medication

9. Mnemonics and Memory Aids

Mnemonics:
  • PVD: Pain, Vascular, Disease
  • ABI: Ankle, Blood, Index
  • STAT: Save, Time, Act, Treat
Memory tricks:
  • Remember the 5 Ps of PVD: pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia
  • Remember the normal range of ABI: 0.9-1.4
